source.label: Beach: Basawan “was also instrumental in the formation of the quite different early Mughal style”

bio.text: Basawan. In back grounding, drawing of features, distribution of colours, portrait painting, and several other branches, he is most excellent, so much so, that many critics prefer him to Daswant’h.
bio.lead: Abu’l Fazl, Akbar’s court historian, ranking the emperor’s painters in the Ain-i Akbari:

source.author: Abu’l Fazl
source.title: Ain-i Akbari, Ain 34: The Art of Painting
source.publisher: translated by H. Blochmann, vol. I, Asiatic Society of Bengal (Internet Archive scan)

bio.text: By 1584, [however], Mir Sayyid Ali was no longer active, Abd as-Samad was a figurehead, and Daswanth had committed suicide. Basawan, therefore, was the most important, prestigious, and influential painter active during the later years of Akbar’s reign.

source.author: Milo Cleveland Beach
source.title: The Imperial Image: Paintings for the Mughal Court
source.publisher: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution (Internet Archive scan)

bio.text: Basawan was a rationalist, with an interest in physical form and texture and a sympathetic [comprehension] of human individuality—unlike his early rival Daswanth, for whom the human was simply one manifestation of a universal energy.

source.author: Milo Cleveland Beach
source.title: The Imperial Image: Paintings for the Mughal Court
source.publisher: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution (Internet Archive scan)
